Justice Dept. Hit with Lawsuit after Refusing to Disclose Rules for Spying on Journalists

Source

The U.S. Department of Justice has refused to reveal its rules for spying on the media, prompting one group representing journalists to sue the agency in federal court.

The Freedom of the Press Foundation filed a lawsuit with the U.S. District Court in San Francisco seeking documents under the Freedom of Information Act that document Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) procedures for issuing national security letters to spy on the media. The Justice Department has so far refused to release the information or even respond to the FOIA request the foundation made in March.

Victoria Baranetsky, the foundation’s attorney, told Courthouse News Service obtaining the records and publishing them “is necessary to deter chilling effects on the press and its sources, especially given recent years during which the Obama Administration has increased surveillance of reporters.”

The Associated Press was targeted by the Justice Department in 2013 when the agency secretly obtained months of phone records for at least seven journalists on 20 phone lines. The administration was trying to learn at the time the source of a government leak regarding Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) work to thwart a terrorist plot.

The Justice Department also investigated Fox News reporter James Rosen in connection with a possible leak of classified information by a government contractor, according to Courthouse News Service.

After these and other such incidents were exposed, the Justice Department created guidelines for prying into the work of journalists. “But the guidelines did not apply to FBI agents using national security letters to get telecom companies, libraries and others to secretly hand over information, including Internet records of U.S. citizens without court oversight,” Elizabeth Warmerdam wrote at Courthouse News Service.

trying to catch up on sleep on the weekends

Unless you're a very special snowflake "catching up on sleep on weekends" is bullshit. Our biological clocks have no concept of weekend and once they settle into a routine you can't just get out of it 2 days a week just because you want to. Some people do sleep a lot on weekends but that doesn't mean they are catching up, it means that they are completely exhausted and don't realize it. Some people can pull it off, but I think it's the vast minority.

The thing is that once you are tired for a long time (weeks, months, years) it's very easy to forget how being not-tired is. You think you're fine but it's just because you forgot what fine really is like. Yes, I'm talking to those people that sleep after 10 minutes watching TV or reading a book - you're not fine. Then these people sleep for 16 hours on Sunday and think they're good to go again - no! Absolutely not! Your body is trying to tell you it's systemically sleep-deprived and instead you think "I've just slept a lot, I guess now it will be fine if I sleep 4 hours a day until next Sunday!"

I hope I'm not being too unclear, it's a weird thing to talk about since it's not a common topic to talk about. Here's another interesting resource that everyone should think about a little bit https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segmented_sleep

Is it really a motivation thing? You don't mention being particularly motivated or unmotivated. I'll treat it as an energy-levels issue, which is what it looks like to me.

I read a great quote recently that said "don't manage your time, manage your energy". I'll let you think what it means for yourself.

A few tips from my own life: I have been identifying my energy-level patterns for a while now and I absolutely know for a fact that if I over-exert myself on the days I'm feeling good then I'll be feeing lazy and tired the next day. Simple physics - if you run out of energy you need to gather energy up again.

Routine is a big factor in maintaining energy levels. If you find yourself a daily routine in which you work (or study or whatever) as much as you rest then your energy levels will be stable every single day. Of course there is no such thing as a perfect routine like this but you can get pretty close to it. You'll also need to think if you really want a everyday routine or if you want to have 4 days a week of light work and 1 of extra-heavy duty. For example: airplane pilots don't work normal schedules because it's really not OK for them to fuck up if they're tired. You need to organize yourself/design your own thing and always adapt when your life changes.

Coffee (or energy drinks and even alcohol) is an available tool that you can use to help settle in your routine. For example: if you want to be very productive during the day you can drink coffee (in moderation, I recommend 2 small cups or 1 expresso at most per day) during the day and then let yourself grow tired and relax at night. If you need to be good-to-go both at day and night better not drink coffee during the day then or you'll be tired at night. Again, if your schedule is weird and you need to be extra productive only twice a week you can drink coffee on those days and not drink any on others. I'm not advocating that you should or not drink coffee or anything else but from experience I know it can help a lot shape up a routine but as with anything it has it's pros and cons.

As other users have said, discipline is paramount. I also recommend learning to clearly separate needs and wants, make schedules and chore list doing at least one productive thing a day. Also know your body's habits. Most people have a time of day where their energy and attention span is the highest, that is the time of day you need to be doing things. You might need to be well feed, or need a nap in the middle of the day to improve your overall performance.
